title: The Future of Libraries Is About More Than Books
author: Carla Hayden
body:
In considering the role of libraries, I’m often pulled to the words of journalist, author, and longtime editor of Saturday Review, Norman Cousins.

“The library is not a shrine for the worship of books,” he wrote in 1954. “It is not a temple where literary incense is burned or one’s devotion to the bound book is expressed in ritual. A library, to modify the famous metaphor of Socrates, should be the delivery room for the birth of ideas—a place where history comes to life.”

Historically, libraries have served as a crucial part of the cultural and civic infrastructure of the nation, responding to local needs and bringing the world to people of all ages. However, in many places today, libraries and library workers are under attack. These attacks are echoes of the past, yet contain a new intensity when libraries are one of the only places where people can go for accurate information and inspiration, while also providing an all-important and free-of-cost “third space” between work and home.

As the 14th Librarian of Congress, as a Senior Fellow at Mellon, and as a librarian whose career spans several decades among various types of libraries, I’ve had the opportunity to work and engage with library workers in all positions. One thing that becomes clear when you talk to librarians today is that libraries must embed themselves in the community, and the community in them. The institutions that will survive are the ones that let their communities shape them.

Across fields, library and cultural workers are taking stock of local experts and leaders, leveraging their libraries as a convener and curator of their local community and its residents.

One approach is to get a strong sense of the skills that people in a community can bring to the table and activate them in times of need. Take disaster preparedness and sustainability. Some libraries are connecting with local beekeepers, gardeners, and arborists, and even more practical and specific sourcing of who might have supplies and tools like chainsaws for when our physical spaces need care. Membership groups like the Sustainable Libraries Initiative are helping library leaders co-create library spaces in this way.

To embed a library into a community and vice versa, many people have spoken to the need to be flexible and to listen. This reflects what library leaders like Shamichael Hallman, author of Meet Me at the Library, mean when he advocates for ensuring that libraries offer “opportunities for shared experiences that allow us to show up and learn from and about each other.”

Libraries are also finding ways to activate and reimagine their collections. People working at the intersections of libraries, archives, and the arts know that archives can sometimes feel static. How can collections be reimagined, recontextualized, and activated to reach more people?

Guggenheim fellow and artist Theaster Gates has explored this idea in relation to the collection of Edward J. Williams, a Chicagoan and keeper of derogatory historical images of Black people. In delicate cases like these, it is critical to preserve objects with care and proper historical context, rather than deaccessioning or erasing them from the record. Gates transformed an abandoned building in Chicago into The Stony Island Arts Bank, which houses approximately 4,000 of these sensitive images from Williams’s collection, exhibits local artists, and provides free weekly screenings of and discussion about films by and about Black people.

There is also real energy around reengaging readers and writers in a hyper-digital age. According to a 2022 report from the National Education Association (NEA), less than half of adults reported having read at least one book in the last year, part of a years-long trend away from deep reading. According to an editorial reviewing research in Psychological Medicine, reading for pleasure is associated with better brain and mental health, stronger cognitive performance, and slower cognitive decline in older adults. Today, libraries are experimenting with creative ways to reengage readers and writers in an increasingly digital age and in the aftermath of the pandemic.

Skye Patrick, director of Los Angeles County Library, who was recently elected the next president of the Public Library Association, has talked about how her library system is reengaging patrons post-pandemic. This includes everything from holding a summit that supports the next generation of writers to redesigning library spaces to be more open and making spaces accessible after hours. “A big part of what libraries currently do and will continue to do is to socialize these changes for people,” Patrick said on an episode of the podcast Live From LA County. “We are the place that literacy lives.”

And at the Columbus Metropolitan Library in Ohio organizers held a day-long program about Black hair: everything from books about hair texture and free haircuts to hair-braiding classes, connecting the stacks to something patrons could feel with their hands.

None of this work happens in isolation. Libraries are learning to work in coalition for the good of the people. Programs like Books Unbanned, a membership program that helps libraries support each other to defend the right to read for teens and young adults, shows what’s possible when institutions choose solidarity and resource sharing over self-preservation or going it alone.

Libraries will survive and thrive if they continue to respond to the needs of all, in partnership with so many others who believe, as former American Library Association Executive Director Tracie Hall has said, that “free people read freely.”
